title: Pathophysiology: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Function—Obstruction, Bleeding and Organ Failure
html:
The gastrointestinal tract must move contents, secrete enzymes and fluid, digest nutrients, absorb water and solutes, maintain a protective barrier, and eliminate waste. The liver, biliary system, and pancreas add metabolic, detoxification, synthetic, immune, and digestive functions. Disorders in this system can rapidly produce hemorrhage, fluid loss, electrolyte disturbance, infection, ischemia, malnutrition, altered consciousness, and multiorgan failure.

Learning goals

  • Relate motility, secretion, digestion, absorption, and barrier function.
  • Explain vomiting, diarrhea, malabsorption, and their fluid and acid–base consequences.
  • Compare mechanical obstruction, ileus, ischemia, perforation, and peritonitis.
  • Recognize gastrointestinal bleeding and compensated or overt shock.
  • Connect hepatocyte injury, fibrosis, portal hypertension, and liver synthetic failure.
  • Explain ascites, varices, coagulopathy, and hepatic encephalopathy.
  • Describe biliary obstruction and acute pancreatitis.
  • Prioritize acute abdomen, hemorrhage, ischemia, sepsis, and liver failure.

Motility, secretion, digestion, and absorption work together

The enteric nervous system, autonomic input, smooth muscle pacemaker activity, local mediators, and gastrointestinal hormones coordinate propulsion and mixing. The mucosal barrier separates a microbe-rich lumen from the circulation while permitting selective absorption. Tight junctions, mucus, bicarbonate, blood flow, immune defenses, and epithelial renewal help maintain this barrier.

Mechanical and enzymatic digestion converts carbohydrates, proteins, and fats into absorbable forms. Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine; the colon recovers water and electrolytes and supports microbial fermentation. Pancreatic enzymes, bile salts, adequate mucosal surface, transit time, and lymphatic and portal transport are all necessary.

Loss of absorptive surface, pancreatic insufficiency, bile-acid disruption, mucosal inflammation, infection, or excessively rapid transit can cause malabsorption. Consequences include weight loss, diarrhea, steatorrhea, anemia, bone disease, vitamin deficiency, edema from protein deficiency, and medication absorption changes.

Vomiting and diarrhea change more than volume

Vomiting removes gastric hydrogen, chloride, potassium, and water and can contribute to volume contraction, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, and secondary potassium loss. Repeated vomiting also increases aspiration, mucosal injury, and acute kidney injury risk. The acid–base pattern may differ if concurrent lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, kidney failure, or intestinal losses are present.

Diarrhea can cause large water, sodium, potassium, and bicarbonate losses, producing volume depletion and normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Secretory diarrhea may continue despite fasting; osmotic diarrhea is driven by poorly absorbed solutes and often improves when the trigger is removed. Inflammatory diarrhea may contain blood, mucus, leukocytes, and protein.

Monitor orthostatic symptoms, perfusion, weight, intake and output, stool or emesis characteristics, kidney function, sodium, potassium, magnesium, bicarbonate, and glucose. Replace losses according to cause and prescribed plan rather than assuming every client needs the same fluid.

The abdominal examination reflects evolving physiology

Pain location, onset, character, migration, aggravating factors, associated symptoms, surgery history, medications, vascular risks, pregnancy possibility, and last stool or flatus help organize hypotheses. Inspect before auscultation and palpation according to local practice, but do not delay urgent escalation to complete a ritualized sequence.

Guarding, rigidity, rebound-type pain, progressive distention, pain with movement, shock findings, or rapidly worsening tenderness suggests peritoneal irritation or advanced injury. Bowel sounds are variable and cannot independently rule in or rule out obstruction, ischemia, or ileus.

Normal-looking early findings can be misleading
Severe pain out of proportion to the initial abdominal examination can occur in mesenteric ischemia. A soft abdomen or present bowel sounds does not make sudden severe pain safe to observe routinely.

Obstruction raises pressure and threatens blood flow

Mechanical obstruction blocks luminal flow at a transition point. Gas, swallowed air, secretions, and fluid accumulate proximally, causing distention, vomiting, third spacing, and electrolyte loss. Rising intraluminal pressure first impairs lymphatic and venous drainage, producing wall edema; continued pressure can compromise arterial flow, causing ischemia, necrosis, bacterial translocation, perforation, and sepsis.

Small-bowel obstruction commonly causes cramping pain, vomiting, distention, and reduced passage of stool or flatus, but partial obstruction may still allow output. Large-bowel obstruction may develop more gradually with marked distention. A closed-loop or strangulated segment has a higher risk of rapid ischemia.

Ileus is functional loss of coordinated propulsion without a mechanical transition point. Surgery, peritonitis, severe illness, opioids, electrolyte disturbance, and autonomic dysfunction can contribute. Mechanical obstruction and ileus require different management and can coexist.

Mesenteric ischemia is a vascular emergency

Acute mesenteric ischemia results from arterial embolism or thrombosis, venous thrombosis, or nonocclusive hypoperfusion and vasoconstriction. Atrial fibrillation, atherosclerosis, heart failure, shock, vasoconstrictive states, and thrombosis risks increase concern. Reduced oxygen delivery injures mucosa first, then deeper bowel layers; reperfusion can add oxidative and inflammatory injury.

Early severe pain may be disproportionate to examination findings. Later findings—distention, guarding, bloody stool, acidosis, rising lactate, fever, and shock—can indicate advanced infarction. Lactate may be normal early and is not an exclusion test. Rapid imaging and surgical or vascular evaluation are time sensitive.

Perforation breaks the barrier

Full-thickness gastrointestinal disruption releases gas, digestive fluid, bacteria, bile, or fecal contents into the peritoneal cavity. Chemical inflammation can rapidly become bacterial peritonitis, capillary leak, sepsis, and shock. Causes include ulcer disease, ischemia, obstruction, diverticular disease, inflammation, trauma, and procedures.

Sudden severe pain, rigid abdomen, worsening tenderness, fever, tachycardia, hypotension, absent or altered bowel function, and free air on imaging are concerning. Keep the client safe from oral intake, support circulation, initiate prescribed sepsis and antimicrobial measures, and prepare for urgent source control.

GI bleeding can be visible, occult, or concealed

Upper-tract bleeding may produce hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena, or rapid hematochezia. Lower bleeding may produce maroon or bright-red stool, but appearance and source overlap. Occult chronic loss may first appear as iron-deficiency anemia, fatigue, or dyspnea.

Heart rate, blood pressure, mental status, skin perfusion, urine output, lactate, and hemoglobin trend help assess severity. Hemoglobin can be initially unchanged during acute blood loss before plasma volume equilibrates, so do not wait for anemia to recognize hemorrhagic shock. Medications—especially anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs, and glucocorticoids—affect risk and response planning.

Priorities include airway protection when bleeding is massive or consciousness declines, large-volume access and laboratory preparation as ordered, hemodynamic monitoring, medication and transfusion protocols, and urgent endoscopic or procedural evaluation. Verify blood products and monitor for treatment complications.

The liver integrates metabolism, synthesis, and detoxification

Hepatocytes regulate carbohydrate, lipid, and amino-acid metabolism; synthesize albumin, clotting factors, transport proteins, and bile; convert ammonia to urea; process bilirubin; and metabolize medications and toxins. The liver also receives portal blood from the gut and participates in immune surveillance.

Markers of hepatocyte injury, such as aminotransferases, do not directly measure remaining synthetic function. Bilirubin, INR, glucose, albumin, mental status, and clinical trends help assess functional consequences, but albumin changes slowly and is influenced by inflammation, nutrition, kidney loss, and distribution.

Fibrosis distorts flow and function

Repeated injury activates inflammatory and stellate-cell pathways, depositing extracellular matrix and creating fibrosis. Progressive architectural distortion forms cirrhosis, increasing resistance within hepatic sinusoids and reducing functional hepatocyte mass. Complications arise from both portal hypertension and loss of liver function.

Portal resistance plus splanchnic vasodilation increases portal pressure and reduces effective arterial volume. Neurohormonal sodium and water retention contributes to ascites and edema. Collateral vessels form at portosystemic connections, creating esophageal or gastric varices and other shunts. Splenic congestion can sequester platelets.

Ascites is not simply excess total-body fluid

Portal hydrostatic pressure, splanchnic vasodilation, renal sodium retention, lymph formation, and reduced oncotic support contribute to ascites. A client can have ascites and edema while intravascular filling and kidney perfusion remain fragile.

Rapid abdominal expansion can impair breathing and mobility. New pain, fever, tenderness, hypotension, kidney dysfunction, or encephalopathy raises concern for infection or decompensation. After large fluid shifts or prescribed drainage, monitor pressure, kidney function, electrolytes, puncture site, and circulatory response.

Variceal bleeding combines hemorrhage and liver vulnerability

Thin-walled portosystemic collaterals can rupture under high portal pressure. Variceal hemorrhage may be massive and can precipitate shock, aspiration, kidney injury, and hepatic encephalopathy. Airway and circulation, prescribed vasoactive and antimicrobial therapy, blood-product strategy, and urgent endoscopic control are coordinated rapidly.

Over-resuscitation can increase portal pressure and worsen bleeding, while under-resuscitation worsens perfusion. Follow condition-specific targets and reassess continuously.

Hepatic encephalopathy is a brain syndrome with multiple contributors

Loss of hepatic clearance and portosystemic shunting allow ammonia and other neuroactive substances to reach systemic circulation. Astrocyte swelling, altered neurotransmission, inflammation, and other metabolic factors contribute. Findings range from sleep and attention changes to confusion, asterixis, somnolence, and coma.

Ammonia may support the diagnosis but does not consistently track clinical severity. Search for and address triggers such as GI bleeding, infection, constipation, dehydration, kidney dysfunction, electrolyte change, sedating medications, or shunt procedures. Protect the airway when consciousness declines and assess for other causes of altered mental status.

Coagulation in liver disease is rebalanced and fragile

The liver synthesizes procoagulant and anticoagulant proteins. Thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, altered fibrinolysis, endothelial changes, and reduced factors create a complex rebalanced state with risk of both bleeding and thrombosis. An elevated INR alone does not fully measure bleeding risk in cirrhosis.

Assess active bleeding, procedure needs, fibrinogen, platelet trend, medications, renal function, and the full clinical context. Correcting a laboratory number without an indication can cause volume overload or thrombosis.

Acute liver failure can progress rapidly

Acute liver failure is abrupt severe hepatic dysfunction in a person without established cirrhosis, characterized by coagulopathy and encephalopathy. Drug toxicity, viral hepatitis, ischemia, autoimmune disease, and other causes can trigger massive hepatocyte injury. Hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, infection, kidney injury, bleeding, cerebral edema, and multiorgan failure may follow.

Review all prescription, over-the-counter, combination, herbal, and recreational exposures and timing. Falling aminotransferases are not necessarily recovery if INR, bilirubin, lactate, glucose, kidney function, or consciousness worsens; enzyme release can fall as viable hepatocyte mass declines.

Biliary obstruction impairs bile flow

Bile carries conjugated bilirubin and supports fat digestion. Obstruction can cause jaundice, dark urine, pale stool, pruritus, and fat malabsorption. Gallstone obstruction may produce biliary colic, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, or ascending cholangitis.

Fever, jaundice, and right-upper-quadrant pain suggest biliary infection; hypotension and altered mentation indicate severe systemic involvement. Source relief and antimicrobial treatment can be urgent.

Acute pancreatitis can become systemic

Premature activation of pancreatic digestive enzymes within acinar cells triggers autodigestion, edema, inflammation, and sometimes necrosis. Gallstones and alcohol are common causes, while medications, very high triglycerides, procedures, trauma, and metabolic factors may contribute.

Severe epigastric pain often radiates to the back and may accompany vomiting, ileus, and tenderness. Capillary leak and inflammatory mediators can produce hypovolemia, acute lung injury, kidney injury, shock, and coagulation abnormalities. Lipase supports diagnosis but does not reliably grade severity.

Management includes prescribed analgesia, appropriate fluid strategy, early nutrition when safe, treatment of the cause, and monitoring for respiratory, renal, circulatory, metabolic, infectious, and local complications. Both insufficient and excessive fluid can be harmful.

Escalate the dangerous pattern
Hematemesis with shock, sudden rigid abdomen, pain out of proportion to examination, obstruction with peritoneal signs, fever and jaundice with hypotension, worsening encephalopathy, or pancreatitis with organ dysfunction requires urgent intervention.

Translate GI and hepatobiliary physiology into clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify pain and timing, distention, emesis, stool and bleeding, last flatus, intake and output, medications, surgery, vascular risk, alcohol and toxin exposure, jaundice, ascites, mental status, perfusion, laboratories, and imaging.
  2. Analyze cues: Organize findings as motility failure, obstruction, ischemia, perforation, inflammation, hemorrhage, malabsorption, biliary blockage, pancreatic injury, portal hypertension, or loss of liver function.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Hemorrhagic shock, bowel ischemia or perforation, strangulated obstruction, cholangitis with sepsis, acute liver failure, severe encephalopathy, and pancreatitis with organ failure outrank stable chronic symptoms.
  4. Generate solutions: Plan ABC support, vascular access and blood preparation, fluid and electrolyte safeguards, bowel rest when indicated, urgent imaging or endoscopy, prescribed medication, source control, and escalation.
  5. Take action: Stabilize the client, maintain aspiration precautions, implement time-sensitive protocols and orders, collect accurate output and specimens, and communicate the trend and likely mechanism.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess pain, abdomen, bleeding, mentation, hemodynamics, urine output, respiratory status, hemoglobin, electrolytes, acid–base balance, kidney and liver function, and treatment harms.

Clinical example

A client with atrial fibrillation develops abrupt severe abdominal pain but has only mild tenderness initially. The RN recognizes possible acute mesenteric ischemia rather than dismissing the mismatch. The RN assesses perfusion and bleeding risk, maintains safety from oral intake, obtains urgent escalation and ordered vascular imaging and laboratories, and trends pain, abdominal findings, lactate, acid–base status, urine output, and hemodynamics. Worsening guarding or shock is communicated immediately.
